  1. (1)T+mv2l
  2. (2)T-mv2l
  3. (3)Zero
  4. (4)T
question.stem: One end of string of length $l$ is connected to a particle of mass ‘$m$’ and the other end is connected to a small peg on a smooth horizontal table. If the particle moves in circle with speed ‘$v$’, the net force on the particle (directed towards center) will be ($T$ represents the tension in the string)

solution.full_text: 1. Centripetal force $\left(\frac{mv^{2}}{l}\right)$ is provided by tension so the net force will be equal to tension i.e., $T$.
solution.html: 1. Centripetal force (mv2l) is provided by tension so the net force will be equal to tension i.e., T.
steps: Centripetal force $\left(\frac{mv^{2}}{l}\right)$ is provided by tension so the net force will be equal to tension i.e., $T$.
printed_lines: the net force will be equal to tension i.e., T.

steps: The table is smooth and horizontal, so the vertical forces cancel: $N = mg$.
The only horizontal force on the particle is the tension $T$ along the string, directed towards the peg (centre).
So the net force towards the centre is $F_{net} = T$, which supplies the centripetal force $T = \frac{mv^{2}}{l}$; this is option $4$.

  3. So the net force towards the centre is Fnet = T, which supplies the centripetal force T = mv2l; this is option 4.
ai_solution.why: On a smooth horizontal table gravity and normal reaction cancel; the only horizontal force is the string tension, so the net force towards the centre is T (= mv^2/l).

question.full_text:
The two nearest harmonics of a tube closed at one end and open at other end are $220\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $260\,\mathrm{Hz}$. What is the fundamental frequency of the system?
(1) $20\,\mathrm{Hz}$
(2) $30\,\mathrm{Hz}$
(3) $40\,\mathrm{Hz}$
(4) $10\,\mathrm{Hz}$
question.html:
The two nearest harmonics of a tube closed at one end and open at other end are 220 Hz and 260 Hz. What is the fundamental frequency of the system?
  1. (1)20 Hz
  2. (2)30 Hz
  3. (3)40 Hz
  4. (4)10 Hz
question.stem: The two nearest harmonics of a tube closed at one end and open at other end are $220\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $260\,\mathrm{Hz}$. What is the fundamental frequency of the system?

solution.full_text:
1. Two successive frequencies of closed pipe
2. $\frac{nv}{4l} = 220$ ...(i)
3. $\frac{(n + 2)v}{4l} = 260$ ...(ii)
4. Dividing (ii) by (i), we get
5. $\frac{n + 2}{n} = \frac{260}{220} = \frac{13}{11}$
6. $11n + 22 = 13n$
7. $n = 11$
8. So, $11\frac{v}{4l} = 220$
9. $\frac{v}{4l} = 20$
10. So fundamental frequency is $20\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
solution.html:
1. Two successive frequencies of closed pipe
  2. nv4l = 220 ...(i)
  3. (n + 2)v4l = 260 ...(ii)
  4. Dividing (ii) by (i), we get
  5. n + 2n = 260220 = 1311
  6. 11n + 22 = 13n
  7. n = 11
  8. So, 11v4l = 220
  9. v4l = 20
  10. So fundamental frequency is 20 Hz.
steps: Two successive frequencies of closed pipe
Dividing (ii) by (i), we get
So fundamental frequency is $20\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
printed_lines: Two successive frequencies of closed pipe

steps: A tube closed at one end supports only odd harmonics: $f = (2n-1)f_0$, i.e. $f_0, 3f_0, 5f_0, \ldots$.
Two nearest (consecutive) harmonics therefore differ by $2f_0$: $260 - 220 = 2f_0$.
$2f_0 = 40\,\mathrm{Hz} \Rightarrow f_0 = 20\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
Check: $\frac{220}{20} = 11$ and $\frac{260}{20} = 13$, both odd, so $f_0 = 20\,\mathrm{Hz}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A tube closed at one end supports only odd harmonics: f = (2n-1)f0, i.e. f0, 3f0, 5f0, ….
  2. Two nearest (consecutive) harmonics therefore differ by 2f0: 260 - 220 = 2f0.
  3. 2f0 = 40 Hz ⇒ f0 = 20 Hz.
  4. Check: 22020 = 11 and 26020 = 13, both odd, so f0 = 20 Hz, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: A closed tube has only odd harmonics, so adjacent harmonics differ by 2f0: 260 - 220 = 40 = 2f0, giving f0 = 20 Hz (220 = 11f0, 260 = 13f0, both odd).

other_options.proof: 10 Hz does divide both printed frequencies, but only as their 22nd and 26th multiples — both EVEN, which a pipe closed at one end cannot sound. The arithmetic available gives 40 (the raw gap) and its half 20 (the key); reaching 10 would need the gap between neighbouring harmonics taken as $4f_0$, and consecutive odd multiples (11 and 13 here) are always $2f_0$ apart, so no step of the standard treatment lands on it.

The fundamental must divide both printed frequencies as an odd multiple. 30 divides neither: $220/30 = 7.33$ and $260/30 = 8.67$. Nor is 30 the gap (40), half the gap (20) or a quarter of it (10), so no arithmetic route from the two printed frequencies reaches it.

The photoelectric threshold wavelength of silver is $3250 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$. The velocity of the electron ejected from a silver surface by ultraviolet light of wavelength $2536 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$ is (Given $h = 4.14 \times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{eVs}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{ms^{-1}}$)
(1) $\approx 0.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{ms^{-1}}$
(2) $\approx 61 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{ms^{-1}}$
(3) $\approx 0.3 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{ms^{-1}}$
(4) $\approx 6 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{ms^{-1}}$

The photoelectric threshold wavelength of silver is 3250 × 10-10 m. The velocity of the electron ejected from a silver surface by ultraviolet light of wavelength 2536 × 10-10 m is (Given h = 4.14 × 10-15 eVs and c = 3 × 108 ms-1)
  1. (1)≈ 0.6 × 106 ms-1

question.stem: The photoelectric threshold wavelength of silver is $3250 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$. The velocity of the electron ejected from a silver surface by ultraviolet light of wavelength $2536 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$ is (Given $h = 4.14 \times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{eVs}$ and $c = 3 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{ms^{-1}}$)

solution.full_text:
1. $\lambda_0 = 3250 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$
2. $\lambda = 2536 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$
3. $\phi = \frac{1242\,\mathrm{eV\text{-}nm}}{325\,\mathrm{nm}} = 3.82\,\mathrm{eV}$
4. $h\nu = \frac{1242\,\mathrm{eV\text{-}nm}}{253.6\,\mathrm{nm}} = 4.89\,\mathrm{eV}$
5. $\mathrm{KE}_{\mathrm{max}} = (4.89 - 3.82)\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.077\,\mathrm{eV}$
6. $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = 1.077 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$
7. $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.077 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}}$
8. $v = 0.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$
solution.html:
1. λ0 = 3250 × 10-10 m
  2. λ = 2536 × 10-10 m
  3. φ = 1242 eV-nm325 nm = 3.82 eV
  4. hν = 1242 eV-nm253.6 nm = 4.89 eV
  5. KEmax = (4.89 - 3.82) eV = 1.077 eV
  6. 12mv2 = 1.077 × 1.6 × 10-19
  7. v = 2 × 1.077 × 1.6 × 10-199.1 × 10-31
  8. v = 0.6 × 106 m/s
steps: $\lambda_0 = 3250 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$
$\lambda = 2536 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$
$\phi = \frac{1242\,\mathrm{eV\text{-}nm}}{325\,\mathrm{nm}} = 3.82\,\mathrm{eV}$
$h\nu = \frac{1242\,\mathrm{eV\text{-}nm}}{253.6\,\mathrm{nm}} = 4.89\,\mathrm{eV}$
$\mathrm{KE}_{\mathrm{max}} = (4.89 - 3.82)\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.077\,\mathrm{eV}$
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.077 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}}$
$v = 0.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m/s}$
$hc = 4.14 \times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{eV\,s} \times 3 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} = 1.242 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{eV\,m}$.
Work function: $\phi_0 = \frac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \frac{1.242 \times 10^{-6}}{3250 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 3.822\,\mathrm{eV}$.
Photon energy: $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{1.242 \times 10^{-6}}{2536 \times 10^{-10}} \approx 4.898\,\mathrm{eV}$.
$K_{max} = 1.076 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J} \approx 1.722 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.
$v = \sqrt{\frac{2K_{max}}{m_e}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.722 \times 10^{-19}}{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}} = \sqrt{3.78 \times 10^{11}} \approx 6.15 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
$6.15 \times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \approx 0.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, which is option $1$ (and equally option $4$, $6 \times 10^{5}$).
ai_solution.html:
1. hc = 4.14 × 10-15 eV s × 3 × 108 m s-1 = 1.242 × 10-6 eV m.
  2. Work function: φ0 = hcλ0 = 1.242 × 10-63250 × 10-10 ≈ 3.822 eV.
  3. Photon energy: E = hcλ = 1.242 × 10-62536 × 10-10 ≈ 4.898 eV.
  4. Kmax = E - φ0 = 4.898 - 3.822 ≈ 1.076 eV.
  5. Kmax = 1.076 × 1.6 × 10-19 J ≈ 1.722 × 10-19 J.
  6. v = 2Kmaxme = 2 × 1.722 × 10-199.1 × 10-31 = 3.78 × 1011 ≈ 6.15 × 105 m s-1.
  7. 6.15 × 105 m s-1 ≈ 0.6 × 106 m s-1, which is option 1 (and equally option 4, 6 × 105).
ai_solution.why: KE = hc(1/lambda - 1/lambda0) = 4.898 - 3.822 = 1.076 eV, so v = sqrt(2KE/m) = 6.15 x 10^5 m/s, i.e. about 0.6 x 10^6 m/s; but option 4 (6 x 10^5) is the same value.

question.full_text:
A spherical black body with a radius of $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ radiates $450\,\mathrm{watt}$ power at $500\,\mathrm{K}$. If the radius were halved and the temperature doubled, the power radiated in watt would be
(1) $450$
(2) $1000$
(3) $1800$
(4) $225$
question.html:
A spherical black body with a radius of 12 cm radiates 450 watt power at 500 K. If the radius were halved and the temperature doubled, the power radiated in watt would be
  1. (1)450
  2. (2)1000
  3. (3)1800
  4. (4)225
question.stem: A spherical black body with a radius of $12\,\mathrm{cm}$ radiates $450\,\mathrm{watt}$ power at $500\,\mathrm{K}$. If the radius were halved and the temperature doubled, the power radiated in watt would be

solution.html:
1. Rate of power loss r ∝ R2T4
  2. r1r2 = R12T14R22T24
  3. = 4 × 116
  4. 450r2 = 14
  5. r2 = 1800 watt
steps: Rate of power loss $r \propto R^{2}T^{4}$
$= 4 \times \frac{1}{16}$
$r_2 = 1800\,\mathrm{watt}$
By the Stefan-Boltzmann law for a black sphere, $P = \sigma (4\pi R^2) T^4$, so $P \propto R^2 T^4$.
$\frac{P'}{P} = \left(\frac{R'}{R}\right)^2 \left(\frac{T'}{T}\right)^4 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 (2)^4$.
$P' = 4 \times 450\,\mathrm{W} = 1800\,\mathrm{W}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. By the Stefan-Boltzmann law for a black sphere, P = σ (4π R2) T4, so P ∝ R2 T4.
  2. P'P = (R'R)2 (T'T)4 = (12)2 (2)4.
  3. (12)2 (2)4 = 14 × 16 = 4.
  4. P' = 4 × 450 W = 1800 W, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Stefan-Boltzmann: P is proportional to R^2 T^4, so P' = 450 x (1/2)^2 x 2^4 = 450 x 4 = 1800 W.

They are brought into contact face to face coinciding the axis of rotation. The expression for loss of energy during this process is
(1) $\frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
(2) $I(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$

  1. (1)14I(ω1 - ω2)2

question.stem: Two discs of same moment of inertia rotating about their regular axis passing through centre and perpendicular to the plane of disc with angular velocities $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$. They are brought into contact face to face coinciding the axis of rotation. The expression for loss of energy during this process is

solution.full_text:
1. $\Delta \mathrm{KE} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{I_1 I_2}{I_1 + I_2}(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
2. $= \frac{1}{2}\frac{I^2}{(2I)}(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
3. $= \frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
solution.html:
1. Δ KE = 12I1 I2I1 + I2(ω1 - ω2)2
  2. = 12I2(2I)(ω1 - ω2)2
  3. = 14I(ω1 - ω2)2
steps: $\Delta \mathrm{KE} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{I_1 I_2}{I_1 + I_2}(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
$= \frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1 - \omega_2)^2$
No external torque acts, so angular momentum is conserved: $I\omega_1 + I\omega_2 = 2I\omega$.
$\omega = \frac{\omega_1 + \omega_2}{2}$.
Initial kinetic energy: $K_i = \frac{1}{2}I\omega_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega_2^2$.
Final kinetic energy: $K_f = \frac{1}{2}(2I)\left(\frac{\omega_1+\omega_2}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1+\omega_2)^2$.
$\Delta K = K_i - K_f = \frac{1}{4}I\left[2\omega_1^2 + 2\omega_2^2 - (\omega_1+\omega_2)^2\right]$.
$\Delta K = \frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1^2 - 2\omega_1\omega_2 + \omega_2^2) = \frac{1}{4}I(\omega_1-\omega_2)^2$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. No external torque acts, so angular momentum is conserved: Iω1 + Iω2 = 2Iω.
  2. ω = ω1 + ω22.
  3. Initial kinetic energy: Ki = 12Iω12 + 12Iω22.
  4. Final kinetic energy: Kf = 12(2I)(ω1+ω22)2 = 14I(ω1+ω2)2.
  5. Δ K = Ki - Kf = 14I[2ω12 + 2ω22 - (ω1+ω2)2].
  6. Δ K = 14I(ω12 - 2ω1ω2 + ω22) = 14I(ω1-ω2)2, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Angular momentum conserved gives common omega = (w1+w2)/2; KE loss = (1/2)I(w1^2+w2^2) - (1/4)I(w1+w2)^2 = (1/4)I(w1-w2)^2.

question.full_text:
A gas mixture consists of 2 moles of $\mathrm{O_2}$ and 4 moles of $\mathrm{Ar}$ at temperature $T$. Neglecting all vibrational modes, the total internal energy of the system is
(1) $15\,RT$
(2) $9\,RT$
(3) $11\,RT$
(4) $4\,RT$
question.html:
A gas mixture consists of 2 moles of O2 and 4 moles of Ar at temperature T. Neglecting all vibrational modes, the total internal energy of the system is
  1. (1)15 RT
  2. (2)9 RT
  3. (3)11 RT
  4. (4)4 RT
question.stem: A gas mixture consists of 2 moles of $\mathrm{O_2}$ and 4 moles of $\mathrm{Ar}$ at temperature $T$. Neglecting all vibrational modes, the total internal energy of the system is

solution.html:
1. U = n1f12RT + n2f22RT
  2. = 2×52RT + 4×32RT
  3. = 5 RT + 6 RT
  4. U = 11 RT
steps: $U = n_1\frac{f_1}{2}RT + n_2\frac{f_2}{2}RT$
$= 2\times\frac{5}{2}RT + 4\times\frac{3}{2}RT$
Neglecting vibration, $\mathrm{O_2}$ (diatomic) has $f = 5$ degrees of freedom and $\mathrm{Ar}$ (monatomic) has $f = 3$.
Internal energy per mole is $U_m = \frac{f}{2}RT$.
$U_{\mathrm{O_2}} = 2 \times \frac{5}{2}RT = 5RT$.
$U_{\mathrm{Ar}} = 4 \times \frac{3}{2}RT = 6RT$.
$U = 5RT + 6RT = 11RT$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Neglecting vibration, O2 (diatomic) has f = 5 degrees of freedom and Ar (monatomic) has f = 3.
  2. Internal energy per mole is Um = f2RT.
  3. UO2 = 2 × 52RT = 5RT.
  4. UAr = 4 × 32RT = 6RT.
  5. U = 5RT + 6RT = 11RT, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: O2 (diatomic, no vibration) has 5/2 RT per mole and Ar (monatomic) 3/2 RT per mole: 2(5/2)RT + 4(3/2)RT = 5RT + 6RT = 11RT.

question.full_text:
The bulk modulus of a spherical object is ‘$B$’. If it is subjected to uniform pressure ‘$p$’, the fractional decrease in radius is
(1) $\frac{B}{3p}$
(2) $\frac{3p}{B}$
(3) $\frac{p}{3B}$
(4) $\frac{p}{B}$
question.html:
The bulk modulus of a spherical object is ‘B’. If it is subjected to uniform pressure ‘p’, the fractional decrease in radius is
  1. (1)B3p
  2. (2)3pB
  3. (3)p3B
  4. (4)pB
question.stem: The bulk modulus of a spherical object is ‘$B$’. If it is subjected to uniform pressure ‘$p$’, the fractional decrease in radius is

solution.full_text:
1. $B = \frac{p}{\left(\frac{\Delta V}{V}\right)}$
2. $\frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{p}{B}$
3. $3\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{B}$
4. $\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{3B}$
solution.html:
1. B = p(Δ VV)
  2. Δ VV = pB
  3. 3Δ rr = pB
  4. Δ rr = p3B
steps: $B = \frac{p}{\left(\frac{\Delta V}{V}\right)}$
$\frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{p}{B}$
$3\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{B}$
$\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{3B}$
Bulk modulus definition: $B = \frac{p}{\Delta V / V}$, so $\frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{p}{B}$.
For a sphere $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, so $\frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3\frac{\Delta r}{r}$.
$3\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{B} \Rightarrow \frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{p}{3B}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Bulk modulus definition: B = pΔ V / V, so Δ VV = pB.
  2. For a sphere V = 43π r3, so Δ VV = 3Δ rr.
  3. 3Δ rr = pB ⇒ Δ rr = p3B, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: B = p/(dV/V) and dV/V = 3 dr/r for a sphere, so dr/r = p/(3B).

Use V = (4/3)pi r^3 for the sphere to relate volumetric strain to radial strain: dV/V = 3 dr/r
Combine the two to get the fractional change in radius as the volumetric strain divided by 3

difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Option p/B is exactly the volumetric strain, so a candidate who stops before converting to radius strain picks it; option 3p/B is the result of multiplying by 3 instead of dividing.

trap.feels: it is the definition rearranged with nothing left over, and both $p$ and $B$ have been used exactly once

steps.text: $B = p/(\Delta V/V)$, so the volume strain is $\Delta V/V = p/B$.
That is the fractional decrease asked for.
steps.fix: The stem asks about the RADIUS: $V = \tfrac43\pi r^3$ gives $\Delta V/V = 3\Delta r/r$, so $\Delta r/r = p/3B$.

Multiplying gives $\Delta r/r = 3p/B$.
steps.fix: The volume strain is the LARGER of the two, three times the radius strain, so the radius strain is $p/3B$ — a radius cannot shrink by more than its volume does.

other_options.who: a student who inverts the definition of a modulus, writing the strain as modulus over stress
other_options.feels: both $B$ and $p$ are pressures, so the quotient is dimensionless either way up and no unit check catches it

Writing the strain as $B/p$ and dividing by 3 gives $B/3p$.
steps.fix: A modulus is stress OVER strain, so strain is stress over modulus; and since $B$ for a solid is far larger than any applied $p$, $B/3p$ would be a fractional decrease bigger than 1.

question.full_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?
((a)) Centre of mass of a body always coincides with the centre of gravity of the body.
((b)) Centre of mass of a body is the point at which the total gravitational torque on the body is zero
((c)) A couple on a body produce both translational and rotational motion in a body.
((d)) Mechanical advantage greater than one means that small effort can be used to lift a large load.
(1) (a) and (b)
(2) (b) and (c)
(3) (c) and (d)
(4) (b) and (d)
question.html:
Which of the following statements are correct?
  1. ((a)) Centre of mass of a body always coincides with the centre of gravity of the body.
  2. ((b)) Centre of mass of a body is the point at which the total gravitational torque on the body is zero
  3. ((c)) A couple on a body produce both translational and rotational motion in a body.
  4. ((d)) Mechanical advantage greater than one means that small effort can be used to lift a large load.
  1. (1)(a) and (b)
  2. (2)(b) and (c)
  3. (3)(c) and (d)
  4. (4)(b) and (d)
question.stem: Which of the following statements are correct?

statements.label: (a)
statements.text: Centre of mass of a body always coincides with the centre of gravity of the body.

statements.label: (b)
statements.text: Centre of mass of a body is the point at which the total gravitational torque on the body is zero

statements.label: (c)
statements.text: A couple on a body produce both translational and rotational motion in a body.

statements.label: (d)
statements.text: Mechanical advantage greater than one means that small effort can be used to lift a large load.

solution.full_text: 1. Centre of mass may or may not coincide with centre of gravity.
solution.html: 1. Centre of mass may or may not coincide with centre of gravity.
steps: Centre of mass may or may not coincide with centre of gravity.
printed_lines: Centre of mass may or may not coincide with centre

steps: (a): $\vec{r}_{CG} = \vec{r}_{CM}$ only when $\vec{g}$ is uniform over the body, so 'always coincides' is false.

(b): In uniform $\vec{g}$, $\vec{\tau}_{CM} = \sum_i \vec{r}_i' \times m_i\vec{g} = \left(\sum_i m_i\vec{r}_i'\right) \times \vec{g} = 0$ since $\sum_i m_i\vec{r}_i' = 0$ about the CM, so (b) is taken as true.
(c): A couple is two equal and opposite forces, so $\vec{F}_{net} = 0$ and there is no translational acceleration; it produces rotation only, so (c) is false.
(d): $MA = \frac{\text{Load}}{\text{Effort}} > 1 \Rightarrow \text{Effort} < \text{Load}$, so (d) is true.
True statements are (b) and (d), which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. (a): →rCG = →rCM only when →g is uniform over the body, so 'always coincides' is false.
  2. (b): In uniform →g, →τCM = ∑i →ri' × mi→g = (∑i mi→ri') × →g = 0 since ∑i mi→ri' = 0 about the CM, so (b) is taken as true.
  3. (c): A couple is two equal and opposite forces, so →Fnet = 0 and there is no translational acceleration; it produces rotation only, so (c) is false.
  4. (d): MA = LoadEffort > 1 ⇒ Effort < Load, so (d) is true.
  5. True statements are (b) and (d), which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: (a) false (CM = CG only in uniform g), (c) false (a couple gives only rotation, net force zero), (d) true; the only option with (d) and without (c) is (b) and (d).

  1. (1)d = 1 km

1. Spring constant ∝ 1length
  2. k ∝ 1l
  3. i.e, k1 = 6k
  4. k2 = 3k
  5. k3 = 2k
  6. In series
  7. 1k' = 16k + 13k + 12k

steps: Spring constant $\propto \frac{1}{\text{length}}$
$k \propto \frac{1}{l}$
In series
For a spring, $k \propto \frac{1}{l}$, so a piece of length $l$ cut from a spring of length $L$ has constant $k\frac{L}{l}$.
The pieces have lengths $\frac{L}{6}, \frac{2L}{6}, \frac{3L}{6}$, so their constants are $k_1 = 6k$, $k_2 = 3k$, $k_3 = 2k$.
Series: $\frac{1}{k'} = \frac{1}{6k} + \frac{1}{3k} + \frac{1}{2k} = \frac{1+2+3}{6k} = \frac{1}{k}$, so $k' = k$.
Parallel: $k'' = 6k + 3k + 2k = 11k$.
$k' : k'' = k : 11k = 1 : 11$, which is option $2$.

1. $F_e = F_g$
2. $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\Delta e^2}{d^2} = \frac{Gm^2}{d^2}$
3. $9 \times 10^{9} (\Delta e^2) = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}$
4. $\Delta e^2 = \frac{6.67 \times 1.67 \times 1.67}{9} \times 10^{-74}$
5. $\Delta e \approx 10^{-37}$
solution.html:
1. Fe = Fg
  2. 14πε0Δ e2d2 = Gm2d2
  3. 9 × 109 (Δ e2) = 6.67 × 10-11 × 1.67 × 10-27 × 1.67 × 10-27
  4. Δ e2 = 6.67 × 1.67 × 1.679 × 10-74
  5. Δ e ≈ 10-37
steps: $F_e = F_g$
$\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\Delta e^2}{d^2} = \frac{Gm^2}{d^2}$
$\Delta e^2 = \frac{6.67 \times 1.67 \times 1.67}{9} \times 10^{-74}$
$\Delta e \approx 10^{-37}$
Each hydrogen atom has a proton $(e + \Delta e)$ and an electron $(-e)$, so its net charge is $\Delta e$.
The two atoms repel electrostatically with $F_e = \frac{k(\Delta e)^2}{d^2}$ and attract gravitationally with $F_g = \frac{G m_h^2}{d^2}$.
Net force zero: $\frac{k(\Delta e)^2}{d^2} = \frac{G m_h^2}{d^2}$, so $\Delta e = m_h\sqrt{\frac{G}{k}}$.
$\frac{G}{k} = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11}}{9 \times 10^{9}} \approx 7.41 \times 10^{-21}$, so $\sqrt{\frac{G}{k}} \approx 8.61 \times 10^{-11}$.
$\Delta e = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times 8.61 \times 10^{-11} \approx 1.44 \times 10^{-37}\,\mathrm{C}$, which is of the order $10^{-37}\,\mathrm{C}$, option $2$.

  2. From Newton's law of gravitation, [G] = [F r2m2] = M-1 L3 T-2.
  3. [Ge24πε0] = M-1 L3 T-2 · M L3 T-2 = L6 T-4.
  4. [Ge24πε0]12 = L3 T-2.
  5. [c2] = L2 T-2, so 1c2[Ge24πε0]12 = L3 T-2L2 T-2 = L.
  6. Check option 2: [e2G 4πε0]12 = (M2)12 = M, and ML2 T-2 = M L-2 T2, not length; options 1 and 3 give L5 T-4 and L5 T-3. So the answer is option 4.
ai_solution.why: G e^2/(4 pi eps0) has dimensions L^6 T^-4; its square root is L^3 T^-2, and dividing by c^2 (L^2 T^-2) leaves L.

chapter.name: Units and Measurements
chapter.why: The answer turns on dimensional analysis: matching the dimensions of c, G and e^2/(4*pi*epsilon_0) to give a quantity with the dimension of length.

subtopics.name: Deducing Relation Among the Physical Quantities Using Dimensional Equation
subtopics.why: The answer comes from setting length proportional to c^a G^b (e^2/4πε0)^c and solving the dimensional equations for the exponents, which is how a relation among physical quantities is deduced with dimensional equations.

step_list: Write the dimensions of the three quantities: c as [L T^-1], G as [M^-1 L^3 T^-2] from Newton's law of gravitation, and e^2/(4*pi*eps0) as [M L^3 T^-2] by recognising it equals force x distance^2 from Coulomb's law
Set length = c^a G^b (e^2/4*pi*eps0)^k and equate the exponents of M, L and T to get three linear equations
Solve the system (mass forces b = k, then the T and L equations fix the exponent of c and the power 1/2) and match the resulting expression to the options
difficulty.why: The work is dimensional analysis: deriving the dimensions of G and of e^2/(4*pi*eps0) from the two inverse-square force laws, then setting up and solving three exponent equations.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The dimensions of e^2/(4*pi*eps0) are not usually memorised and must be derived from Coulomb's law; the options differ only in the sign of the exponent of c, whether G multiplies or divides, and whether the square root is taken, so a single sign or exponent slip lands on a distractor.

steps.text: $e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0$ is $\mathrm{kg\,m^3s^{-2}}$ and $G$ is $\mathrm{m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}}$, so their product is mass-free and its root is $\mathrm{m^3s^{-2}}$.
Multiplying by $c^2$ then gives the length.
steps.fix: Multiplying adds $\mathrm{m^2s^{-2}}$ and gives $\mathrm{m^5s^{-4}}$; dividing by $c^2$ removes it and leaves $\mathrm{m}$.

steps.text: $G$ times $e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0$ has no kilogram in it, which is the first thing a length must satisfy.
Dividing that product by $c$ then gives a length.
steps.fix: The product is $\mathrm{m^6s^{-4}}$, the square of $\mathrm{m^3s^{-2}}$, so the root comes first; one power of $c$ can never reduce $\mathrm{m^6s^{-4}}$ to $\mathrm{m}$.

other_options.who: a student who removes $G$ by dividing, the way an unwanted constant is usually cleared
other_options.feels: $\sqrt{e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 G}$ is a combination seen before - it is a mass - so the expression looks like a known one, and the $1/c^2$ matches the right answer

steps.text: $G$ has to be combined with $e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0$ so that the kilogram disappears.
Putting $G$ in the denominator does that job.
steps.fix: $G$ carries $\mathrm{kg^{-1}}$ and the electric factor carries $\mathrm{kg}$, so they must MULTIPLY to cancel; dividing gives $\mathrm{kg^2}$ under the root, and the option ends up as a mass over $c^2$.

categories.reason: This question requires combining three given constants into something with the dimensions of length, demonstrated by 'A physical quantity of the dimensions of length that can be formed out of $c$, $G$ and $e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0$'.
categories.note: All four options are built from the same three ingredients, so the question is settled only by a full dimensional check; the three wrong ones are the three distinct misplacements - $c^2$ in the numerator, $G$ in the denominator, and the square root omitted - which is why each carries a route and none is a filler.

question.full_text:
Two Polaroids $P_1$ and $P_2$ are placed with their axis perpendicular to each other. Unpolarised light $I_0$ is incident on $P_1$. A third polaroid $P_3$ is kept in between $P_1$ and $P_2$ such that its axis makes an angle $45^\circ$ with that of $P_1$. The intensity of transmitted light through $P_2$ is
(1) $\frac{I_0}{4}$
(2) $\frac{I_0}{8}$
(3) $\frac{I_0}{16}$
(4) $\frac{I_0}{2}$

  1. (1)I04
  2. (2)I08
  3. (3)I016
  4. (4)I02

A third polaroid $P_3$ is kept in between $P_1$ and $P_2$ such that its axis makes an angle $45^\circ$ with that of $P_1$. The intensity of transmitted light through $P_2$ is

solution.full_text:
[Figure: Polaroids P1, P3, P2 on a light beam with their axes meeting P1's axis at 45° and 90°]
1. $I_2 = \frac{I_0}{2}\cos^2 45^\circ$
2. $= \frac{I_0}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}$
3. $= \frac{I_0}{4}$
4. $I_3 = \frac{I_0}{4}\cos^2 45^\circ$
5. $I_3 = \frac{I_0}{8}$
solution.html:
1. I2 = I02cos2 45°
  2. = I02 × 12
  3. = I04
  4. I3 = I04cos2 45°
  5. I3 = I08

spec.title: Polaroids P1, P3, P2 on a light beam with their axes meeting P1's axis at 45° and 90°

steps: Unpolarised light through $P_1$: $I_1 = \frac{I_0}{2}$.
Through $P_3$ at $45^\circ$ to $P_1$ (Malus's law): $I_2 = I_1 \cos^2 45^\circ = \frac{I_0}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{I_0}{4}$.
Angle between $P_3$ and $P_2$ is $90^\circ - 45^\circ = 45^\circ$.
Through $P_2$: $I_3 = I_2 \cos^2 45^\circ = \frac{I_0}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{I_0}{8}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Unpolarised light through P1: I1 = I02.
  2. Through P3 at 45° to P1 (Malus's law): I2 = I1 cos2 45° = I02 × 12 = I04.
  3. Angle between P3 and P2 is 90° - 45° = 45°.
  4. Through P2: I3 = I2 cos2 45° = I04 × 12 = I08, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Unpolarised light is halved by P1, then Malus's law with cos^2 45 = 1/2 applies twice (P1 to P3, P3 to P2), giving I0/8.

trap.label: arithmetic_slip
trap.route: The chain is stopped one sheet short: the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ at $P_1$ and one $\cos^2 45^\circ$ at $P_3$ give $I_0/4$, which is the intensity leaving $P_3$ and not the intensity leaving $P_2$
trap.who: a student who knows Malus's law and applies it sheet by sheet, but counts one $45^\circ$ gap where the setup has two
trap.feels: the stem prints only one angle, $45^\circ$ between $P_3$ and $P_1$, so one $\cos^2 45^\circ$ looks like the whole angular story

steps.text: Unpolarised $I_0$ through $P_1$ leaves $I_0/2$.
$P_3$ is at $45^\circ$ to $P_1$, so $(I_0/2)\cos^2 45^\circ = I_0/4$ leaves $P_3$.
$I_0/4$ is what reaches $P_2$, so $I_0/4$ is the transmitted intensity.
steps.fix: $P_2$ sits at $45^\circ$ to $P_3$ as well, so one more $\cos^2 45^\circ$ applies and the answer is $I_0/8$.

other_options.who: a student who remembers the demonstration that light reappears when a third polaroid is slipped between two crossed ones, but not how much of it reappears
other_options.feels: the one factor they are sure of is the half an unpolarised beam loses at the first sheet, and the $45^\circ$ sheet is remembered as restoring the beam

steps.text: $P_1$ passes $I_0/2$ of the unpolarised beam.
The $45^\circ$ sheet restores transmission through the crossed pair, so $I_0/2$ comes out of $P_2$.
steps.fix: The restoration costs a $\cos^2 45^\circ$ at $P_3$ and another at $P_2$, so what comes out is a quarter of $I_0/2$, namely $I_0/8$.

other_options.proof: $I_0/16$ needs four factors of $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and the setup supplies three: $\tfrac{1}{2}$ at $P_1$, $\cos^2 45^\circ$ at $P_3$, $\cos^2 45^\circ$ at $P_2$. Dropping one or two of them gives $I_0/4$ or $I_0/2$, and reading $\cos^2 45^\circ$ as $\tfrac{1}{4}$ gives $I_0/32$; no route built from the stem's numbers lands on $I_0/16$.

question.full_text:
A particle executes linear simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of $3\,\mathrm{cm}$. When the particle is at $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the mean position, the magnitude of its velocity is equal to that of its acceleration. Then its time period in seconds is
(1) $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2\pi}$
(2) $\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{5}}$
(3) $\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}$
(4) $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{\pi}$
question.html:
A particle executes linear simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 3 cm. When the particle is at 2 cm from the mean position, the magnitude of its velocity is equal to that of its acceleration. Then its time period in seconds is
  1. (1)52π
  2. (2)4π5
  3. (3)2π3
  4. (4)5π
question.stem: A particle executes linear simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of $3\,\mathrm{cm}$. When the particle is at $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the mean position, the magnitude of its velocity is equal to that of its acceleration. Then its time period in seconds is

solution.full_text:
1. $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$
2. $a = x\omega^2$
3. $v = a$
4. $\omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = x\omega^2$
5. $\sqrt{(3)^2 - (2)^2} = 2\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)$
6. $\sqrt{5} = \frac{4\pi}{T}$
7. $T = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{5}}$
solution.html:
1. v = ωA2 - x2
  2. a = xω2
  3. v = a
  4. ωA2 - x2 = xω2
  5. (3)2 - (2)2 = 2(2πT)
  6. 5 = 4πT
  7. T = 4π5
steps: $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$
$a = x\omega^2$
$v = a$
$\omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2} = x\omega^2$
$\sqrt{(3)^2 - (2)^2} = 2\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)$
$\sqrt{5} = \frac{4\pi}{T}$
$T = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{5}}$
In SHM the speed at displacement $x$ is $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$.
With $A = 3$ and $x = 2$: $v = \omega\sqrt{9 - 4} = \sqrt{5}\,\omega$.
The acceleration magnitude is $a = \omega^2 x = 2\omega^2$.
Setting $|v| = |a|$: $\sqrt{5}\,\omega = 2\omega^2 \Rightarrow \omega = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{5}/2} = \frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{5}}\,\mathrm{s}$, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In SHM the speed at displacement x is v = ωA2 - x2.
  2. With A = 3 and x = 2: v = ω9 - 4 = 5 ω.
  3. The acceleration magnitude is a = ω2 x = 2ω2.
  4. Setting |v| = |a|: 5 ω = 2ω2 ⇒ ω = 52.
  5. T = 2πω = 2π5/2 = 4π5 s, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: At x = 2 cm, |v| = omega*sqrt(A^2 - x^2) = omega*sqrt(5) and |a| = omega^2*x = 2*omega^2; equating gives omega = sqrt(5)/2, so T = 2*pi/omega = 4*pi/sqrt(5) s.

step_list: Write the SHM speed at displacement x = 2 cm with amplitude A = 3 cm: v = omega*sqrt(A^2 - x^2) = omega*sqrt(5)
Write the SHM acceleration magnitude at x = 2 cm: a = omega^2 * x = 2*omega^2
Equate the two magnitudes to solve for omega, then convert to time period with T = 2*pi/omega
difficulty.why: The work is recalling the two standard SHM relations for speed and acceleration as functions of displacement, equating them to get the angular frequency, and converting that to the period.

trap.label: formula_misused
trap.route: The condition $|v|=|a|$ is solved correctly for $\omega=\sqrt5/2$ and then the link between $\omega$ and the period is written upside down, so $\omega$ lands on top of $\pi$: $\sqrt5/2\pi$ instead of $4\pi/\sqrt5$
trap.who: a student who stores "$\omega=2\pi/T$" and "$T=2\pi/\omega$" as one fraction without fixing which quantity is underneath
trap.feels: $\sqrt5$ is the number their own algebra produced, so an option carrying $\sqrt5$ reads as their answer, and the $\pi$ underneath looks like the usual $1/2\pi$ conversion

steps.text: At $x=2$ cm, $|v|=\omega\sqrt{3^2-2^2}=\omega\sqrt5$ and $|a|=\omega^2\cdot 2$.
Equating them gives $\omega=\sqrt5/2$ rad s$^{-1}$.
The period is $\omega$ divided by $\pi$, which is $\sqrt5/2\pi \approx 0.36$ s.
steps.fix: $T=2\pi/\omega$: $\omega$ goes underneath $2\pi$, so $T=2\pi\div(\sqrt5/2)=4\pi/\sqrt5\approx 5.6$ s.

other_options.who: a student who reaches $\omega=\sqrt5/2$ and then builds the period out of the pieces $\sqrt5$, $2$ and $\pi$ by inspection rather than from $T=2\pi/\omega$
other_options.feels: $\sqrt5/\pi$ is the same inverted shape with the $2$ of $\omega$ kept upstairs, and it still carries the $\sqrt5$ the condition produced

steps.text: $\omega\sqrt5=2\omega^2$ gives $\omega=\sqrt5/2$.
Writing the period as $2\omega/\pi$ gives $\sqrt5/\pi\approx 0.71$ s.
steps.fix: Check the units of the shape: $2\pi/\omega$ has seconds, $\omega/\pi$ has s$^{-1}$, so $\pi$ must sit on top.

other_options.proof: $2\pi/\sqrt3$ keeps the correct shape $T=2\pi/\omega$ but needs $\omega=\sqrt3$, and the printed numbers give $3^2-2^2=5$, hence $\omega=\sqrt5/2$. A radicand of $3$ arises only if the displacement is taken as $1.5$ cm, half the amplitude, and the stem prints "at $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ from the mean position"; no slip on $9-4$ produces $3$ either.

categories.note: None of the three distractors is the exact output of one named slip in the physics: options 1 and 4 are exactly $\omega/\pi$ and $2\omega/\pi$, i.e. the $\omega$-to-$T$ relation written upside down, which is why the trap is placed on that family; option 3 keeps the right shape with a radicand the stem's numbers cannot produce.

solution.full_text:
1. $h_{\mathrm{oil}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{oil}}\,g = h_{\mathrm{water}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{water}}\,g$
2. $140 \times \rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = 130 \times \rho_{\mathrm{water}}$
3. $\rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = \frac{13}{14} \times 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$
4. $\rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = 928\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$
solution.html:
1. hoil ρoil g = hwater ρwater g
  2. 140 × ρoil = 130 × ρwater
  3. ρoil = 1314 × 1000 kg/m3
  4. ρoil = 928 kg m-3
steps: $h_{\mathrm{oil}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{oil}}\,g = h_{\mathrm{water}}\,\rho_{\mathrm{water}}\,g$
$140 \times \rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = 130 \times \rho_{\mathrm{water}}$
$\rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = \frac{13}{14} \times 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$
$\rho_{\mathrm{oil}} = 928\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$
Water drops $65\,\mathrm{mm}$ on the oil side and rises $65\,\mathrm{mm}$ on the other, so the water column above level $BC$ is $h_w = 65 + 65 = 130\,\mathrm{mm}$.
The oil top stands $10\,\mathrm{mm}$ above the final water level, so the oil column is $h_o = 130 + 10 = 140\,\mathrm{mm}$.
Pressures at $B$ and $C$ (same level, same liquid below) are equal: $P_a + \rho_o g h_o = P_a + \rho_w g h_w$.
$\rho_o = \rho_w \frac{h_w}{h_o} = 1000 \times \frac{130}{140} \approx 928\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Water drops 65 mm on the oil side and rises 65 mm on the other, so the water column above level BC is hw = 65 + 65 = 130 mm.
  2. The oil top stands 10 mm above the final water level, so the oil column is ho = 130 + 10 = 140 mm.
  3. Pressures at B and C (same level, same liquid below) are equal: Pa + ρo g ho = Pa + ρw g hw.
  4. ρo = ρw hwho = 1000 × 130140 ≈ 928 kg m-3, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Equal pressures at level B-C: oil column 140 mm balances water column 130 mm, so rho_oil = 1000 x 130/140 = 928 kg m^-3.

solution.full_text:
1. $w_g + w_a = K_f - K_i$
2. $mgh + w_a = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2} - 0$
3. $10^{-3} \times 10 \times 10^{3} + w_a = \frac{1}{2} \times 10^{-3} \times (50)^{2}$
4. $w_a = -8.75\,\mathrm{J}$ i.e. work done due to air resistance and work done due to gravity $= 10\,\mathrm{J}$
solution.html:
1. wg + wa = Kf - Ki
  2. mgh + wa = 12mv2 - 0
  3. 10-3 × 10 × 103 + wa = 12 × 10-3 × (50)2
  4. wa = -8.75 J i.e. work done due to air resistance and work done due to gravity = 10 J

steps: Work done by gravity: $W_g = mgh = (10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg})(10\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(10^{3}\,\mathrm{m}) = 10\,\mathrm{J}$.
Final kinetic energy (starting from rest): $K_f = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(10^{-3})(50)^2 = 1.25\,\mathrm{J}$.
Work-energy theorem: $W_g + W_r = K_f - 0$.
$W_r = 1.25\,\mathrm{J} - 10\,\mathrm{J} = -8.75\,\mathrm{J}$, so (i) $10\,\mathrm{J}$ and (ii) $-8.75\,\mathrm{J}$, which is option $3$.

3. $v_{x} = 5 - 4t \qquad v_{y} = 10$
4. $\frac{dv}{dt}x = -4 \qquad \frac{dv}{dt}y = 10$
5. $a_{x} = -4 \qquad a_{y} = 0$
6. Acceleration of particle at $t = 2\,\mathrm{s}$ is $= -4\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$

Differentiate y = 10t twice with respect to time to get the y-component of acceleration
Combine the two components into the net acceleration and note it does not depend on t, so the value at t = 2 s follows directly
difficulty.why: The work is two second-derivative calculations, one for each coordinate, followed by combining the components, and recognising that the given time does not enter.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: One option equals the x-velocity's time-dependent term (-4t) evaluated at t = 2 s, which is what a candidate gets by differentiating only once and substituting the given time; the stated t = 2 s invites that substitution.

The acceleration is the $-4t$ part, so at $t=2$ it is $-8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
steps.fix: Differentiate a second time: $a_x = \mathrm{d}v_x/\mathrm{d}t = -4\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, with no $t$ left to substitute.

question.full_text:
A long solenoid of diameter $0.1\,\mathrm{m}$ has $2 \times 10^{4}$ turns per meter. At the centre of the solenoid, a coil of $100$ turns and radius $0.01\,\mathrm{m}$ is placed with its axis coinciding with the solenoid axis. The current in the solenoid reduces at a constant rate to $0\,\mathrm{A}$ from $4\,\mathrm{A}$ in $0.05\,\mathrm{s}$. If the resistance of the coil is $10\pi^{2}\,\Omega$, the total charge flowing through the coil during this time is
(1) $16\,\mu\mathrm{C}$
(2) $32\,\mu\mathrm{C}$
(3) $16\pi\,\mu\mathrm{C}$
(4) $32\pi\,\mu\mathrm{C}$

question.stem: A long solenoid of diameter $0.1\,\mathrm{m}$ has $2 \times 10^{4}$ turns per meter. At the centre of the solenoid, a coil of $100$ turns and radius $0.01\,\mathrm{m}$ is placed with its axis coinciding with the solenoid axis. The current in the solenoid reduces at a constant rate to $0\,\mathrm{A}$ from $4\,\mathrm{A}$ in $0.05\,\mathrm{s}$. If the resistance of the coil is $10\pi^{2}\,\Omega$, the total charge flowing through the coil during this time is

solution.full_text:
1. $\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\phi}{dt}$
2. $\left|\frac{\varepsilon}{R}\right| = \frac{N}{R}\frac{d\phi}{dt}$
3. $dq = \frac{N}{R}d\phi$
4. $\Delta Q = \frac{N(\Delta\phi)}{R}$
5. $\Delta Q = \frac{\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{total}}}{R}$
6. $= \frac{(NBA)}{R}$
7. $= \frac{\mu_{0} n i \pi r^{2}}{R}$
8. Putting values
9. $= \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 100 \times 4 \times \pi \times (0.01)^{2}}{10\pi^{2}}$
10. $\Delta Q = 32\,\mu\mathrm{C}$
solution.html:
1. ε = -Ndφdt
  2. |εR| = NRdφdt
  3. dq = NRdφ
  4. Δ Q = N(Δφ)R
  5. Δ Q = ΔφtotalR
  6. = (NBA)R
  7. = μ0 n i π r2R
  8. Putting values
  9. = 4π × 10-7 × 100 × 4 × π × (0.01)210π2
  10. Δ Q = 32 μC
steps: $\varepsilon = -N\frac{d\phi}{dt}$
$\left|\frac{\varepsilon}{R}\right| = \frac{N}{R}\frac{d\phi}{dt}$
$dq = \frac{N}{R}d\phi$
$\Delta Q = \frac{N(\Delta\phi)}{R}$
$\Delta Q = \frac{\Delta\phi_{\mathrm{total}}}{R}$
$= \frac{(NBA)}{R}$
$= \frac{\mu_{0} n i \pi r^{2}}{R}$
Putting values
$= \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 100 \times 4 \times \pi \times (0.01)^{2}}{10\pi^{2}}$
$\Delta Q = 32\,\mu\mathrm{C}$
Inside the long solenoid the field is $B = \mu_0 n I$, uniform over the small coil.
The coil area is $A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.01)^2 = \pi \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$.
Total flux linkage change: $\Delta(N\Phi) = N \mu_0 n \Delta I A = 100 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2 \times 10^{4} \times 4 \times \pi \times 10^{-4} = 3.2\pi^2 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Wb}$.
Charge flowed: $Q = \frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{R} = \frac{3.2\pi^2 \times 10^{-4}}{10\pi^2} = 3.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C}$.
$Q = 32\,\mu\mathrm{C}$, which is option $2$.

1. Inside the long solenoid the field is B = μ0 n I, uniform over the small coil.
  2. The coil area is A = π r2 = π (0.01)2 = π × 10-4 m2.
  3. Total flux linkage change: Δ(NΦ) = N μ0 n Δ I A = 100 × 4π × 10-7 × 2 × 104 × 4 × π × 10-4 = 3.2π2 × 10-4 Wb.
  4. Charge flowed: Q = Δ(NΦ)R = 3.2π2 × 10-410π2 = 3.2 × 10-5 C.
  5. Q = 32 μC, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Charge Q = N*dPhi/R with B = mu0*n*I through the coil area pi*r^2: Q = 100*4pi*10^-7*2*10^4*4*pi*10^-4/(10pi^2) = 32 microC.

chapter.name: Electromagnetic Induction
chapter.why: The answer turns on Faraday's law of induction giving the charge through the coil as change in flux linkage divided by resistance (Q = N*delta(phi)/R), which is electromagnetic induction; the solenoid field B = mu0*n*I is only a supporting input.

subtopics.name: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
subtopics.why: The answer uses the Faraday's-law result that the charge through the coil equals the total flux change divided by resistance (q = N*mu0*n*dI*pi*r^2/R = 32 microC), where that flux is the solenoid's field linked to the inner coil (a mutual-induction setup).

step_list: Find the field inside the long solenoid from B = mu0 n I and its change as the current falls from 4 A to 0
Find the change in flux linkage through the inner coil as N B pi r^2, using the coil's radius (0.01 m), not the solenoid's diameter
Use induced charge q = (change in flux linkage) / R, which does not depend on the time, and substitute so the pi^2 cancels against the 10 pi^2 ohm resistance
difficulty.why: The work is to chain the solenoid field formula to the flux linkage through a smaller coaxial coil, then apply q = delta(Phi)/R and evaluate with the pi factors cancelling.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Redundant data: the solenoid diameter and the 0.05 s interval are given but not needed, so a candidate must recognise that the coil's own area sets the flux and that the charge does not depend on time. The options differ only by a factor of 2 or of pi, so a dropped pi from the area or from mu0 lands on a listed option.

source.note: Read from image. Text layer draft dropped the pi and Omega in the resistance (image: 10π² Ω), dropped the μ and π in the options (image: 16 μC, 32 μC, 16π μC, 32π μC), and had a stray trailing 'd' after 'is' that is not in the image. No stacked fraction bar is visible in the crop; the flagged fraction appears to be a text-layer artifact.

categories.concept: The charge that flows through a closed coil is $q = N\,\Delta\Phi/R$, which depends on the total flux change and not on how long the change takes

trap.label: arithmetic_slip
trap.route: The flux carries $\pi$ twice — once from $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}$ and once from $A=\pi r^2$ — and only one of them is cancelled against the $10\pi^2\,\Omega$ resistance, leaving a stray $\pi$ and $32\pi\,\mu\mathrm{C}$
trap.who: a student who sets up $q = N\mu_0 n\,\Delta I\,\pi r^2/R$ correctly and then cancels the $\pi$s by eye instead of collecting them
trap.feels: the resistance is printed as $10\pi^2\,\Omega$, so an answer still carrying a $\pi$ looks like the natural outcome of dividing by it

steps.text: $\Delta\Phi$ per turn $= \mu_0 n\,\Delta I\cdot\pi r^2 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2\times10^{4}\times4\times\pi\times10^{-4}$, so $N\Delta\Phi = 32\pi^2\times10^{-5}$ Wb.
Dividing by $10\pi^2$ leaves one $\pi$: $3.2\pi\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C} = 32\pi\,\mu\mathrm{C}$.
steps.fix: The numerator holds $\pi^2$, not $\pi$, so the $\pi^2$ in $10\pi^2$ cancels it completely and $q = 32\,\mu\mathrm{C}$.

other_options.who: a student who uses the average current during the decay instead of the change in current, carrying over the habit from average-emf questions
other_options.feels: the current "reduces at a constant rate to $0\,\mathrm{A}$ from $4\,\mathrm{A}$", so the mean value $2\,\mathrm{A}$ reads as the current that counts

steps.text: $q = N\Delta\Phi/R$ with $\Delta\Phi$ built from $\mu_0 n\,\pi r^2$.
Put the average current $(4+0)/2 = 2\,\mathrm{A}$ in place of the current change, halving everything to $16\,\mu\mathrm{C}$.

question.full_text:
A Carnot engine having an efficiency of $\frac{1}{10}$ as heat engine, is used as a refrigerator. If the work done on the system is $10\,\mathrm{J}$, the amount of energy absorbed from the reservoir at lower temperature is
(1) $90\,\mathrm{J}$
(2) $99\,\mathrm{J}$
(3) $100\,\mathrm{J}$
(4) $1\,\mathrm{J}$
question.html:
A Carnot engine having an efficiency of 110 as heat engine, is used as a refrigerator. If the work done on the system is 10 J, the amount of energy absorbed from the reservoir at lower temperature is
  1. (1)90 J
  2. (2)99 J
  3. (3)100 J

question.stem: A Carnot engine having an efficiency of $\frac{1}{10}$ as heat engine, is used as a refrigerator. If the work done on the system is $10\,\mathrm{J}$, the amount of energy absorbed from the reservoir at lower temperature is

solution.html:
1. β = 1-ηη
  2. = 1-110110 = 910110
  3. β = 9
  4. β = Q2W
  5. Q2 = 9 × 10 = 90 J
steps: $\beta = \frac{1-\eta}{\eta}$
$\beta = 9$
$\beta = \frac{Q_2}{W}$
$Q_2 = 9 \times 10 = 90\,\mathrm{J}$
Carnot efficiency: $\eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{1}{10}$, so $\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{9}{10}$.
Coefficient of performance of the same cycle run as a refrigerator: $\beta = \frac{T_2}{T_1 - T_2} = \frac{1-\eta}{\eta}$.
Heat absorbed from the cold reservoir: $Q_2 = \beta W = 9 \times 10\,\mathrm{J} = 90\,\mathrm{J}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Carnot efficiency: η = 1 - T2T1 = 110, so T2T1 = 910.
  2. Coefficient of performance of the same cycle run as a refrigerator: β = T2T1 - T2 = 1-ηη.
  3. β = 9/101/10 = 9.
  4. Heat absorbed from the cold reservoir: Q2 = β W = 9 × 10 J = 90 J, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: For a reversible Carnot cycle, COP of refrigerator = (1 - eta)/eta = 9, so heat absorbed from cold reservoir Q2 = 9 x 10 J = 90 J.

step_list: Use eta = 1 - T2/T1 = 1/10 to get the reservoir temperature ratio T2/T1 = 9/10 (the reversed Carnot engine works between the same reservoirs)
Recall the refrigerator coefficient of performance beta = Q2/W = T2/(T1 - T2), equivalently (1 - eta)/eta, and evaluate it from the ratio
Multiply beta by the work input of 10 J to get the heat Q2 absorbed from the cold reservoir
difficulty.why: The work is linking the given heat-engine efficiency to the refrigerator coefficient of performance through the reservoir temperatures, then one multiplication by the work input.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Option 100 J is exactly W/eta, the heat delivered to the hot reservoir, so a candidate who confuses Q1 with Q2 (or applies the engine relation directly) lands on a printed option.

categories.concept: A Carnot engine run backwards as a refrigerator: the efficiency fixes the hot-reservoir heat from the work, $Q_1 = W/\eta$, and the cold reservoir gives up what is left once the work is taken out, $Q_2 = Q_1 - W$

With $W = 10\,\mathrm{J}$ that gives $Q_1 = 100\,\mathrm{J}$.
Reads $100\,\mathrm{J}$ off as the energy absorbed and stops.
steps.fix: The stem asks for the reservoir at LOWER temperature, so take the work back out: $Q_2 = Q_1 - W = 100 - 10 = 90\,\mathrm{J}$.

steps.fix: Efficiency is work out over heat in, so heat is $W/\eta$, not $\eta W$; a refrigerator moves more heat than the work fed to it, so any answer below $10\,\mathrm{J}$ is the fraction used upside down.

other_options.proof: Worked every value the stem's two numbers reach on a single wrong move: $W/\eta = 100$, $\eta W = 1$, $W/\eta - W = 90$, $W(1-\eta)/\eta = 90$, $W/\eta + W = 110$, $W/(1-\eta) = 11.1$. None lands on 99. The only arrival at 99 needs two errors at once and they contradict each other: use $W = 10$ to get $Q_1 = 100$, then subtract $\eta W = 1$ as though the work were $1\,\mathrm{J}$. It sits one unit under the 100 J distractor as spread.
